article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica-dominant hybrid
Genetics: GMO × Double Burger
Breeder: Skunk House Genetics
THC Content: 25–32%
CBD Content: Low to trace
Terpene Profile: caryophyllene , limonene , myrcene
Primary Flavors: Garlic, diesel, savory herbs, black pepper
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–9 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: late September to early October
Indoor Yield: Medium to high
Outdoor Yield: High
Grow Difficulty: Moderate to advanced

Triple Burger takes the pungent side of modern marijuana breeding to an extreme. Instead of balancing GMO genetics with fruit, candy, or dessert flavors, Skunk House Genetics crossed GMO back into Double Burger, a related Burger-family cultivar already saturated with GMO influence. The resulting plant, sometimes described as GMO BX3, concentrates the garlic, Chem, diesel, earthy funk, and heavy resin production that made this genetic family famous.

Skunk House Genetics openly identifies itself with the “Burger Funk” family of cannabis breeding, and Triple Burger is one of the clearest examples of that direction. Its aroma can fill a room with a peculiar combination of crushed garlic, fuel, black pepper, damp earth, skunk, and savory food-like notes. Potency is equally serious. Commercial examples have tested around 30% THCA with terpene levels above 3%, placing this cultivar firmly in territory best approached by experienced cannabis consumers.
Genetics and Lineage

Triple Burger is GMO × Double Burger, bred by Skunk House Genetics. That deceptively simple formula represents several generations of intentional backcrossing around GMO. Double Burger itself is GMO × Donny Burger, while Donny Burger comes from GMO × Han Solo Burger . Because Han Solo Burger also contains GMO ancestry, Triple Burger repeatedly returns to the same Chem-and-Cookies foundation rather than moving outward toward unrelated genetics. Prime Cuts Nursery’s documented Burger-family genealogy identifies Triple Burger specifically as GMO × Double Burger from Skunk House Genetics.

The original GMO foundation traces to Chem D and Forum Cookies , while the Burger branch adds Larry OG influence through Han Solo Burger. That repeated genetic concentration explains why the finished weed can express such an unusually forceful savory profile. Garlic, onion-like funk, fuel, pepper, chemical sharpness, and Kush earthiness appear repeatedly throughout the family tree. The objective was clearly not subtlety. Triple Burger represents a deliberate reinforcement of the traits that distinguished GMO from the fruit-forward cannabis varieties surrounding it.

This genetic concentration also helps explain the plant’s value for extraction. GMO and Donny Burger have both earned reputations for abundant trichome production, while Burger-family cultivars are widely used for solventless hash . Triple Burger continues that tendency with sticky flowers capable of carrying substantial cannabinoid and terpene concentrations. Cannara’s commercial Triple Burger hash rosin , produced from GMO × Double Burger flower, lists limonene, caryophyllene, myrcene, and farnesene among its major aromatic compounds.
Effects and Experience

The opening minutes can be deceptive. Triple Burger may initially produce a distinct cerebral shift, with mood elevation, a slight euphoric buzz, and enough mental stimulation to make conversation, music, or entertainment more absorbing. That early phase prevents the strain from feeling completely one-dimensional despite its strongly indica-leaning reputation. Some batches can even produce a brief energetic or creative window before the physical component takes over.

Once the high develops fully, the character becomes much heavier. Relaxation spreads through the body, eyelids can begin to feel weighted, and the desire to remain active usually decreases. Rather than creating a sharp crash, the cultivar often seems to progressively turn down physical and mental intensity. Evening television, gaming, listening to music, or simply settling into a comfortable chair fit the experience better than complicated tasks requiring fast reactions or sustained concentration.

Potency can dramatically alter that progression. Licensed Triple Burger flower from Skyworld has tested around 29.95% THC with 2.71% total terpenes, while another commercial batch reached 30.16% THCA and 3.03% terpenes. At those levels, an amount that feels relaxing to an experienced cannabis consumer can become overwhelming for someone with limited tolerance. High doses may produce significant sleepiness, impaired short-term memory, dry mouth, dry eyes, dizziness, or anxiety.
Medical Benefits

Triple Burger may appeal to medical marijuana patients who prefer a strong, physically relaxing cannabis profile during the latter part of the day. People sometimes choose cultivars with this type of effect progression when temporary discomfort, muscular tension, reduced appetite, stress, or difficulty winding down interferes with rest. The initial mood lift can make the transition into relaxation feel less abrupt than with weed that produces immediate sedation.

Its chemistry varies by producer, but several laboratory-tested batches show a recurring group of terpenes. A 2024 Triple Burger flower analysis measured 2.69% total terpenes, led by myrcene at approximately 0.76%, limonene at 0.64%, beta-caryophyllene at 0.62%, and humulene at 0.27%. Another licensed batch was caryophyllene-dominant, followed by myrcene and limonene. These compounds help explain the peppery, earthy, citrus, and herbal character of the flower, but terpene content alone cannot predict a specific medical response.

Triple Burger itself has not been clinically demonstrated to treat insomnia, chronic pain, anxiety, depression, or another medical disorder. Patients should rely on the cannabinoid and terpene analysis of the particular product being considered rather than assuming every batch is chemically identical. Anyone using prescription medications or managing significant medical conditions should discuss high-THC cannabis with an appropriate healthcare professional.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Triple Burger is among the least dessert-like weed strains to carry a food-themed name. Garlic and fuel dominate the first impression, often accompanied by a powerful skunky quality that becomes stronger when the flower is ground. Beneath that surface are black pepper, earth, herbs, and an almost buttery or fatty richness. Some expressions develop ammonia-like sharpness, while others resemble onion, fermented vegetation, coffee, or savory meat. Skyworld describes its tested flower with garlic gas, pepper, earthy funk, diesel, and meaty notes, an unusually accurate summary of the cultivar’s broader aromatic direction.

Smoking or vaporizing the flower reveals more contrast. Pepper and sour gas can strike early, followed by deeper garlic and herbal flavors across the middle of the palate. Limonene-rich batches occasionally provide enough citrus brightness to break through the heavier funk, although the fruitiness never becomes the main event. Caryophyllene and humulene contribute a dry, spicy quality, while myrcene can reinforce the musky earth underneath.

The finish can linger considerably longer than the initial inhale, leaving behind garlic, fuel, spice, and a slightly chemical note. Consumers who primarily enjoy strawberry, candy, cream, or tropical cannabis may find Triple Burger unusually aggressive. For anyone drawn to Chem, GMO, garlic, skunk, and diesel profiles, however, that lack of sweetness is precisely the attraction.
Growing Information

Triple Burger is a photoperiod marijuana cultivar with an approximately eight-to-nine-week breeder flowering window. The plants can show substantial stretch during the transition into bloom, a trait inherited from the GMO-heavy family, so indoor growers should account for final height before changing the light schedule. Topping during vegetative growth and spreading branches with low-stress training can produce a more manageable canopy while creating additional productive flowering sites.

Once buds begin accumulating weight, structural support becomes increasingly useful. Trellis netting or stakes can keep branches positioned beneath the strongest light while preventing mature colas from leaning into neighboring plants. Removing weak lower growth before the later stages of flowering can also improve airflow and direct resources toward the upper canopy. The objective should be an open plant with enough circulation to protect dense, resinous flowers rather than a crowded mass of foliage.

Humidity deserves close attention during the final weeks. Thick Burger-family buds and heavy trichome coverage can create favorable conditions for mold when air remains stagnant. Growers should maintain consistent circulation through the canopy and avoid dramatic humidity spikes as maturity approaches. Outdoor cultivation is best suited to locations receiving abundant direct sunlight and relatively dry conditions toward the end of the season. A late-September to early-October harvest is a reasonable planning range in many Northern Hemisphere environments, but actual readiness should always be determined from flower and trichome maturity.

The post-harvest period matters just as much as flowering. Drying the buds too quickly can flatten the pungent garlic and chemical-gas aromatics, while excessive warmth can drive off volatile terpenes. A controlled dry followed by a gradual cure allows the savory layers to become clearer and can soften the harsh edges of freshly harvested weed.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Triple Burger?

Triple Burger is GMO × Double Burger and was bred by Skunk House Genetics. Because Double Burger is itself GMO × Donny Burger and Donny Burger contains additional GMO ancestry, Triple Burger is essentially an intensive continuation of the GMO genetic family.
Is Triple Burger indica or sativa?

Triple Burger is an indica-dominant hybrid. The high can begin with noticeable cerebral stimulation or euphoria, but the experience usually becomes increasingly relaxing and physically heavy as it progresses.
How strong is Triple Burger?

It is generally high-potency cannabis. Commercial batches commonly fall in the mid-to-upper 20% range, while licensed flower has tested around 30% THC or THCA. One current example measured 29.95% THC, and another tested at 30.16% THCA.
What does Triple Burger taste like?

Garlic, diesel, black pepper, earth, herbs, skunk, and savory funk form the core flavor profile. Some batches add buttery, chemical, onion-like, or mildly citrus notes, but sweet fruit generally remains secondary.
How long does Triple Burger take to flower?

The breeder’s documented flowering range is approximately eight to nine weeks, with around 60 days frequently cited for faster expressions. Actual plants can require additional time depending on phenotype and growing conditions, so trichome maturity should determine harvest rather than the calendar alone.
Final Thoughts on Triple Burger

Triple Burger is less a departure from GMO than an attempt to concentrate everything that made GMO unusual in the first place. Skunk House Genetics combined GMO with Double Burger, stacking several generations of related Chem, Cookies, Burger, and OG genetics into a plant that delivers dense resin production and one of the more aggressively savory terpene profiles found in modern marijuana. Garlic, diesel, pepper, skunk, earth, and chemical funk dominate where many contemporary hybrids rely on candy sweetness.

The high follows the same uncompromising approach. A brief period of cerebral elevation can appear at the beginning, but deep physical relaxation increasingly takes control, particularly with today’s high-testing commercial flower. Combined with strong trichome production and proven appeal in solventless concentrates, those characteristics make Triple Burger valuable to consumers, growers, and hash makers alike. For cannabis enthusiasts who consider loud garlic-and-gas weed more appealing than another sugary dessert strain, Triple Burger is one of the definitive expressions of the modern Burger family.
